UP PLAYBOOK 2026
CD-S-002
Corporate Communications Strategy
Strategy Building scope. Sibling workflow to CD-S-001.
Version 1.0 | April 2026
Owner: Chief Strategy Officer
Approver: CEO
Note. This workflow follows the same template structure as CD-S-001 and references it for common elements. Where CD-S-002 says "as per CD-S-001," that material is identical. Where it differs, the differences are explicit and material — that's where corporate strategy work meaningfully diverges from brand work.
Section 1 — Identification
Section 2 — Purpose & Scope
Purpose. To produce a client-approved corporate communications strategy that defines how the company (not its individual brands) will build, protect, and grow its reputation with all material stakeholders — investors, regulators, employees, media, government, NGOs, customers, partners, and the public — through integrated communications across earned, owned, shared, and selectively paid channels.
A corporate strategy at UP is PR-centric, stakeholder-led, reputation-driven. It is the highest-stakes work UP does because corporate reputation directly affects company valuation, license to operate, employee engagement, and commercial outcomes. The 2026 UP deck explicitly cites that brand and corporate reputation can account for 15% to 30% of a company's total valuation — and up to 40% for companies with strong identity and trust. That number is the value at stake in this workflow.
In scope
Corporate reputation strategies for established companies (e.g. Diageo as the parent of Johnnie Walker; Melexis as a corporate; VMware as the regional employer and innovator)
Repositioning of the corporate identity (e.g. post-merger, post-leadership-change, post-crisis)
Annual corporate communications strategy refresh for retained clients
Corporate strategy work for B2B companies where the company is the brand (e.g. SAAB, Fadata, Linamar, Kyndryl)
Corporate strategy for Bulgarian companies expanding internationally (intersects with CD-S-004 Market Entry)
Corporate strategy for international companies entering or scaling in the markets UP serves
Out of scope
Brand-level strategy → use CD-S-001 Brand Communications Strategy
Strategies that must address brand and corporate together → use CD-S-003 Integrated Alignment
Pure public affairs / regulatory engagement strategies → use CD-S-010 Public Affairs Strategy (which can also nest as a component here)
Live crisis events → use CD-E-013 Crisis Live Response
Pitch-stage corporate work for prospects → compressed pitch workflow
Mode clarification
Corporate Communications Strategy is standalone-only. It defines the overall reputation objective and stakeholder universe; it cannot be a component of another strategy. The dual-mode strategies that nest inside a Corporate Strategy as components are listed in Section 5 Step 3.3.
When to use this workflow
A new corporate client signs UP for reputation work
An existing retainer client commissions an annual corporate strategy refresh
A material corporate event invalidates the existing strategy: M&A, leadership change, restructuring, IPO/delisting, regulatory action, ESG transition, geopolitical exposure
A standalone corporate engagement is commissioned (e.g. positioning around a major investment, reputation rebuild, ESG transition)
The client faces a multi-stakeholder challenge that brand-level work cannot solve
When NOT to use this workflow
Single-product or single-brand work — use CD-S-001
Tactical media engagement around a specific moment without underlying strategy — use CD-E-004 Media Relations Planning & Execution
Issues management without strategic context — use CD-E-013 Crisis Live Response if live, or CD-S-007 Crisis Preparedness if proactive
Section 3 — Inputs
Largely as per CD-S-001, with the following corporate-specific additions and elevations:
Quality gate principle, intensified. For corporate work, input quality directly correlates with strategic accuracy. A brand strategy with weak inputs produces mediocre work. A corporate strategy with weak inputs produces dangerously wrong work — recommendations that fail under regulatory scrutiny, stakeholder pushback, or analyst challenge. Strategy Lead has hard veto authority on input quality.
Section 4 — Roles & RACI
Largely as per CD-S-001, with these corporate-specific elevations:
Two key clarifications corporate strategy demands
Senior leadership is non-optional. A corporate strategy without senior co-leadership is a brand strategy mislabeled. UP's CEO and CSO are part of the product the client is buying.
Legal must be in the loop early on regulated work. Late legal review at the end of Phase 4 has killed otherwise good corporate strategies. For regulated clients, legal is consulted at insight definition, not just at presentation.
Section 5 — Process Steps
The five-phase structure of CD-S-001 holds, but the content of each phase shifts substantially. The biggest differences are in Phase 2 (research goes deeper into stakeholders and regulatory context), Phase 3 (the components and frameworks differ), and Phase 4 (legal and ethical review is heavier).
Phase 1 — Immersion & Discovery (Week 1)
As per CD-S-001 Phase 1, with these adjustments:
Step 1.1 Client kickoff must include the corporate decision-maker (CEO, CommsDir, or board sponsor), not only working-level contacts. If the decision-maker is unavailable for kickoff, kickoff is rescheduled, not held without them. This is a hard rule.
Step 1.3 Background immersion explicitly includes: annual reports, investor calls and transcripts, analyst reports, employee survey data, regulatory filings, prior crisis records, and any pending or recent legal matters. AI summarization is permitted within Section 9 boundaries — typically much narrower for corporate clients than for brand.
New step 1.5 — Legal & compliance context briefing. For regulated, listed, or high-stakes clients, the Strategy Lead briefs legal counsel (internal client legal or external) on the engagement and confirms what cannot be communicated externally during the strategy period. Establishes the disclosure perimeter early.
Phase 2 — Research & Insight (Weeks 1–4, longer than brand)
This is where corporate strategy diverges most sharply from brand strategy. Research is deeper, broader, more stakeholder-oriented, and more rigorous.
Step 2.1 — Business & operating context audit
(Replaces "category audit".) Financial performance, operating model, geographic footprint, M&A history, governance, ESG posture, regulatory exposure, key risks disclosed in annual report. Output: business and operating context summary.
Step 2.2 — Stakeholder universe mapping
(Elevated and expanded vs CD-S-001.) The most important phase of corporate research. Comprehensive identification and segmentation:
The deliverable uses the influence/interest grid for prioritization. Output: comprehensive stakeholder map.
Step 2.3 — Reputation audit
Detailed assessment of current corporate reputation across stakeholder groups. Sources include: media coverage analysis (volume, sentiment, narratives, share of voice vs competitors), social listening across professional platforms (LinkedIn, X, sector forums) and general platforms, analyst sentiment, employee engagement scores if available, customer satisfaction data if available, NGO and regulatory commentary. Sensika and Media Zoom configured for corporate-mode listening (different from brand-mode). Output: reputation audit deck.
Step 2.4 — Competitive corporate audit
Reputation, narrative, ESG positioning, executive visibility, thought leadership posture, and crisis history of 3–5 named corporate peers. Distinct from brand competitive audit. Output: competitive corporate audit.
Step 2.5 — Regulatory & policy environment scan
Critical and corporate-specific. What regulatory, legislative, and policy developments will shape the company's operating environment over the strategy period? Coordinated with FTI Consulting or CEC Group via UP's public affairs partnerships when relevant. Output: regulatory & policy memo.
Step 2.6 — Issues & vulnerability scan
What are the company's foreseeable reputation vulnerabilities? Past issues, ongoing litigation, sector controversies, ESG exposures, leadership exposures, geographic risk, supply chain risk, AI/data exposure (a 2026 universal). This is not crisis preparedness (CD-S-007) — this is strategic awareness of the vulnerability landscape that the strategy must address. Output: vulnerability register.
Step 2.7 — Cultural & geopolitical scan
For 2026, geopolitical context (energy transition, supply chain reshoring, EU regulatory leadership, US-China dynamics, defense reorientation in CEE) is integral to corporate strategy. Trends, cultural forces, and political shifts that will shape the company's operating reality. Output: cultural and geopolitical memo.
Step 2.8 — Insight synthesis
Strategy Lead synthesizes all research into 1–3 corporate insights that will drive the strategy. Corporate insights typically take the form of "what tension does this company need to resolve in the eyes of its stakeholders to grow / protect itself / earn license to operate?" The insight is always human-defined, never AI-generated. Output: corporate insight statement(s) logged in Insight Library.
Decision Point: Re-brief or proceed?
Same as CD-S-001 but with elevated stakes. If research reveals the original brief was wrong or incomplete on corporate matters — particularly if a material risk or regulatory issue surfaces that the client did not disclose at kickoff — the Strategy Lead pauses and re-engages the client. Proceeding with undisclosed material risk is not just a workflow failure; it's a professional ethics issue.
Phase 3 — Strategy Development (Weeks 4–6)
Step 3.1 — Strategic positioning
Define the company's strategic positioning across stakeholders. Different from a brand proposition — corporate positioning answers "what does this company stand for, deliver, and protect?" rather than "what does this brand mean to consumers?" Output: corporate positioning one-pager.
Step 3.2 — Corporate narrative & messaging architecture
Multi-track architecture, not single-message:
Master corporate narrative (one)
Audience-specific message tracks (per stakeholder segment — investor message track, employee message track, media message track, regulator message track, etc.)
Proof points per track
Tone of voice per track (regulator-facing language is not media-facing language)
"Do not say" guardrails — explicit messages to avoid for legal, regulatory, or reputational reasons
Output: messaging framework with multi-track architecture.
Step 3.3 — Stakeholder engagement approach — the Required Components
Where brand strategies are PESO-led, corporate strategies are stakeholder-led. Each stakeholder segment gets an explicit engagement approach. The required components for a corporate strategy are:
The components matrix is the quality checklist. A corporate strategy missing a required component is not complete.
Step 3.4 — Reputation measurement framework
Different from brand measurement. The framework typically combines:
Reputation tracking (RepTrak, brand-specific tracker, or commissioned tracking)
Share of voice and sentiment in tier-1 business media
Stakeholder-specific KPIs (analyst sentiment, employee engagement, regulator relationship indicators, NGO sentiment)
Issues resilience metrics
Executive visibility metrics
Thought leadership impact (citations, speaker invitations, content engagement)
Crisis-readiness indicators
Aligned to AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 (2025) and the AMEC Integrated Evaluation Framework (IEF), but with a corporate framework rather than a brand framework. Mixed quantitative and qualitative methods are required (Barcelona Principle 3); AVEs are explicitly excluded (Barcelona Principle 4); outputs, outcomes and impact must all be reported (Barcelona Principle 5); and ethics, governance and transparency in data and methodology are documented (Barcelona Principle 6). Output: corporate measurement framework.
Step 3.5 — Phased budget allocation
Corporate budgets typically skew earned and owned, with selective paid for executive thought leadership and major moments. Production costs (research papers, content hubs, signature events) are often substantial and need explicit treatment. Output: budget table.
Step 3.6 — Risk register & mitigation
More extensive than for brand work. Strategic risks, reputational risks, regulatory risks, legal risks, ethical risks, geopolitical risks. Output: risk register.
Step 3.7 — Annual roadmap
Twelve-month corporate calendar showing major moments (results announcements, investor days, AGM, sustainability report publication, executive appearances, signature events, anticipated regulatory milestones), plus always-on activity. Output: roadmap.
Step 3.8 — Internal alignment plan
Corporate-specific: how will this strategy be socialized inside the client organization? Who needs to buy in beyond the immediate sponsor? Corporate strategies fail more often from internal misalignment than from external rejection. Output: internal alignment plan.
Phase 4 — Internal Review & Packaging (Week 6–7)
As per CD-S-001 Phase 4, with these elevations:
Internal challenge session is mandatory and senior-led. CEO and CSO co-lead the challenge for all corporate strategies. For flagship corporate engagements, an external senior advisor may be invited.
New step — Legal review. For regulated, listed, or high-stakes corporate strategies, the strategy is reviewed by legal counsel before client presentation. Specifically: disclosure perimeter compliance, MNPI considerations, regulatory positioning, litigation posture coherence.
New step — Ethical review. For corporate strategies touching geopolitical, defense, healthcare, public-sector, or politically sensitive matters, an explicit ethical review by a senior reviewer not involved in drafting. This is a real and increasingly important governance step in 2026.
Phase 5 — Client Presentation & Approval (Week 7–8)
As per CD-S-001 Phase 5, with these elevations:
Client presentation is to the decision-maker (CEO or board sponsor), not only the Communications Director.
CEO of UP attends in person for new corporate clients, flagship engagements, or strategies above the value threshold.
Approval is in writing, formally archived. Corporate strategy approval is signed-document-grade, not email-grade.
Internal client launch. Corporate strategies require an internal launch within the client organization. UP supports this — typically through an internal launch deck, town hall support, and an internal Q&A pack.
Handover triggers. As per CD-S-001, plus typically multiple component-mode strategies (CD-S-007 Crisis, CD-S-008 Employer, CD-S-011 Executive Profiling, CD-S-012 CSR) trigger downstream depending on the components.
Section 6 — Outputs & Deliverables
Section 7 — Systems & Tools
As per CD-S-001, with these corporate-specific notes:
Sensika and Media Zoom configured for corporate listening — different keyword sets, different sources, different dashboards from brand-mode. Set up at engagement start; don't reuse a brand listening config for corporate work.
Bloomberg, Reuters, FT, S&P / Moody's databases — for listed clients, access to financial intelligence sources is required for credible work.
LinkedIn Sales Navigator and equivalent — for stakeholder mapping at named-individual level.
Approved AI tools for corporate work — narrower list than brand work. Some clients restrict AI tool use to EU-hosted only, named-providers only. The #AI-status field in the project file is set per client and enforced strictly.
Section 8 — AI Augmentation
The pattern from CD-S-001 holds, but the AI permissiveness is materially lower for corporate work.
AI today — what UP does in corporate work
Document summarization — annual reports, regulatory filings, analyst reports synthesized into immersion memos. Strategist validates anything entering the strategy.
Stakeholder universe research acceleration — initial stakeholder identification from public sources.
Reputation audit synthesis — themes extracted from media and social listening data.
Regulatory environment scanning — initial scan accelerated; legal-relevant interpretation always human and where warranted, lawyer-validated.
Drafting support — narrative drafts, deck copy. Always human-authored in final form.
Insight stress-testing — AI as a thinking partner challenging assumptions.
AI next — corporate-specific roadmap
Continuous reputation monitoring with stakeholder-specific signal detection (E: H, I: H). Move from monthly audit to continuous monitoring with early warning for stakeholder-specific risks.
Analyst sentiment tracking automation for listed clients (E: M, I: H).
Regulatory development tracking with semantic alerting (E: H, I: H). Critical for regulated clients in 2026.
Stakeholder-specific message tracking — does the messaging architecture actually land with each segment? AI-assisted analysis of received vs intended messages.
Synthetic stakeholder simulation — testing messages with simulated stakeholder personas before exposure. Higher value but also higher risk; deploy carefully.
Human-in-the-loop requirements — even firmer than for brand
The corporate insight is always human and always defended by senior judgment. Corporate insights affect company valuation and license to operate. AI proposes; humans decide and own.
Anything stakeholder-facing is human-reviewed. Every word, every visual, every framing. No exceptions.
Material non-public information (MNPI) is never processed in AI tools. For listed clients, this is a legal requirement, not a preference.
Regulatory and legal recommendations require legal review — not just human review. For regulated work, a non-lawyer human reviewing legal-relevant content is not sufficient governance.
Ethical review is mandatory for corporate strategies touching geopolitical, defense, public-sector, healthcare, or politically sensitive matters.
#noAI variant is the default for: listed clients during quiet periods, M&A engagements, regulated-sector clients with restrictive contracts, public-sector clients, defense clients, and any client who has explicitly opted out.
Audit trail is mandatory and elevated. Prompt logs retained for the contract duration plus 7 years (longer than brand workflow's 3 years), reflecting the longer regulatory and legal tail of corporate work. Aligned with Barcelona Principle 7 — ethics, governance and transparency with data, methodologies and technology builds trust and drives learning.
Failure modes specific to corporate AI use — and they're severe
MNPI leak via AI prompt — career-ending and potentially regulatory.
Hallucinated regulatory citation in a strategy document — exposes UP and the client to sanction.
AI-generated "executive voice" content that doesn't match the executive — visible, embarrassing, and undermines trust at exactly the wrong level.
Stakeholder data processed without proper consent — GDPR and ePrivacy exposure.
Cross-client MNPI exposure — Client A's listed-company information surfaces in Client B's work. Catastrophic.
These risks are why corporate AI use at UP is conservative by design.
Section 9 — Data & Compliance
Data classifications handled
Most corporate strategy work defaults to Restricted.
M&A, pre-results-period, IPO/delisting, restructuring, and major regulatory engagements default to Highly Restricted.
Public-sector, defense, and healthcare work frequently elevates to Highly Restricted.
MNPI handling for listed clients
Quiet periods enforced — strategy work paused or limited around results announcements per the client's disclosure calendar.
AI tool use restricted or prohibited during quiet periods.
Need-to-know access enforced — corporate strategy team for listed clients is a named, limited group.
All team members on listed-client work confirm in writing they understand MNPI obligations. Logged annually.
GDPR considerations for corporate work
Stakeholder mapping at named-individual level requires GDPR-compliant handling.
Employee research and engagement data is high-sensitivity.
Cross-border data flows in multi-market corporate work require explicit safeguards.
EU AI Act alignment, 2026
Most corporate communications work is limited-risk under the AI Act.
Engagement of high-risk AI use (e.g. influencing democratic processes, biometric stakeholder analysis, profiling for discriminatory targeting) is prohibited at UP regardless of client request. Hard line.
Transparency obligations: where AI is used in stakeholder-facing content, that fact is appropriately disclosed per client and UP policy.
Sectoral overlays
Healthcare clients — pharmaceutical advertising and disease awareness regulations vary by market; legal review at minimum at insight definition.
Defense clients — export control and security classification considerations override AI tool use; #noAI is default.
Financial services / listed clients — MNPI as above, plus market abuse considerations.
Public-sector clients — procurement compliance, freedom-of-information considerations, political neutrality.
Energy clients — regulated tariff communications, environmental disclosure, ESG materiality.
Cross-reference
Full data and AI governance lives in CD-REF-003 Data & AI Governance Policy. This workflow notes corporate-specific elevations only.
Section 10 — KPIs & Quality Standards
Efficiency KPIs
Quality KPIs
Business KPIs
The quality standard — a corporate strategy is "good" when:
It clearly identifies the reputation problem or opportunity at company level
It has a defensible human insight that resolves a real stakeholder tension
The stakeholder universe is comprehensive and prioritized
The messaging architecture is multi-track and stakeholder-tailored
All Required Components are present
The measurement framework reflects reputation, not activity
The risk register is comprehensive and mitigations are credible
It survived senior internal challenge
It received legal review where required and ethical review where required
It addresses internal alignment, not just external communications
It is signed off by the corporate decision-maker, not by a delegate
It would withstand scrutiny from analysts, regulators, journalists, or NGOs if it became public

Section 14 — Changelog
End of CD-S-002
Two strategy gold standards now established. CD-S-001 covers brand. CD-S-002 covers corporate. Together they set the methodology, governance, and quality bar for the remaining 10 strategy workflows. Subsequent strategy workflows can be written more efficiently because the structural patterns, the dual-mode handling, the AI governance approach, and the KPI framework are now consistent across the strategy scope.

# Real Client Case For AI Workflow Demo

Selected case: Corporate brand strategy, built from scratch

Client: A real United Partners telecom client, sanitized. No client name is used.

Status: Sanitized, confidential, for AI workflow demo.

## Short Ask

This case is a corporate brand and corporate communications strategy built from a blank slate. The client has no approved corporate brand strategy, and positioning, narrative, and pillar architecture are not pre-decided. The workflow must reason from evidence to a defensible strategy and show what is fact, what is missing, and what is strategic judgment.

## Client Type

Industry/category: Telecommunications: fixed line, mobile, broadband internet, TV/entertainment, and B2B solutions such as IoT, smart cities, cloud, and digital education.

Market/country: A single mid-sized European national market. The client is a subsidiary of a larger regional telecoms-and-media group.

B2B or B2C: Both. Mass-market consumer is the revenue core. B2B, enterprise, and public-sector solutions are strategic growth areas.

Current business situation: Market leader by revenue and the incumbent operator. Operationally strong, with leading network, fixed infrastructure, and entertainment assets. Stable and profitable, but operating in a mature, saturated, price-pressured market where the three main operators have converged on near-identical positioning. The company operates beyond core connectivity, but is not yet recognized for that broader role.

## Real Challenge

Trigger: A leadership transition requiring a narrative reset. The specific transition details are excluded from AI use.

What the client wants to change: Move from reactive, campaign-by-campaign communications to one coherent corporate brand strategy. The client must decide on a corporate positioning and narrative that do not currently exist in approved form. Prior agency proposals were liked but never adopted, so the company is effectively starting fresh.

Business/reputation problem:

- Differentiation: the three main operators recycle technology leadership, ESG, and employer-brand claims.
- Affinity: the category is trusted but not loved.
- Contested leadership: share of voice has moved from clear dominance to a tight race.
- Latent strength: national scale, infrastructure, digital-economy role, CSR, and skills programmes exist, but are communicated as episodes rather than one corporate story.

## Objectives

- Re-establish corporate reputation and leadership trust after the transition.
- Build a differentiated corporate brand platform the market can recognize.
- Lift affinity and preference in a trusted-but-not-loved category.
- Strengthen employer brand for digital and engineering talent.
- Establish credible, ownable ESG and societal-contribution leadership.

## Audiences To Prioritize

These audiences are not pre-ranked. The strategy must prioritize them.

- Media: national news, business/financial press, tech media, consumer media.
- Regulators, policy stakeholders, and government stakeholders.
- Talent and future talent: students, STEM graduates, tech community.
- Business and enterprise customers and partners.
- General public and consumer base.
- Parent-group corporate stakeholders.

## Must-Say And Must-Avoid

Because positioning is open, these are guardrails, not the message itself.

Must-say guardrails:

- Use verifiable and ownable proof.
- Show a genuine role in the country’s digital progress.
- Build one company story rather than disconnected activity claims.

Must-avoid guardrails:

- Do not fall back into state-utility or former-monopoly framing.
- Do not recycle shared category claims around technology leadership, ESG, or employer branding as the central idea.
- Do not use competitive price-war messaging as corporate positioning.
- Do not introduce political framing.

## Decision Setup

Primary approval owner: client-side Corporate Communications lead.

Final sign-off: CEO and parent-group corporate communications function.

Consulted teams: Marketing, HR/People, Product, Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and parent-group communications.

Internal alignment tension: Marketing owns consumer brand and advertising budget. Corporate Communications owns reputation and PR. The corporate platform must sit above and feed consumer campaigns without colliding with them. Parent-group requirements add an approval layer. Because positioning is genuinely undecided, the strategy must force and document the positioning decision the client still owes itself.

## Competitive And Market Context

Main competitors: two strong rivals in a three-player market. One is positioned around technology/network leadership and social-impact programming. The other is positioned around customer experience and independently certified network quality. Both invest heavily in corporate narrative and are closing the share-of-voice gap.

Reference brands: major European incumbent operators that repositioned from utility to digital enabler. These are directional benchmarks only, not targets to copy.

Market pressure: mature, saturated, price-competitive market; streaming pressure on traditional TV consumption; convergence pressure from over-the-top players. Growth must come from preference and value, not volume.

Known audience-perception problem: the category is trusted but not admired. The client is respected for reliability and scale but is not associated with a distinctive idea. Competitors out-narrate it on innovation and customer experience, while the client’s relative strength appears more in corporate, sustainability, and CSR coverage than product buzz.

Open strategic question: Is incumbent scale and infrastructure a liability to move away from, or, retold in human and national terms, the one position rivals cannot match? The strategy must take a view; the brief must not assume one.

## Channels And Components

PESO direction:

- Earned: core driver for corporate reputation.
- Owned: newsroom, reports, internal channels, and thought-leadership content.
- Shared: professional social, executive social, consumer social where relevant.
- Paid: supporting role only.
- Partnerships, CSR, and ESG: high relevance.
- Crisis sensitivity: regulatory proceedings, outages, data security, and leadership-transition sensitivities.

## Constraints

Legal/regulatory:

- The client operates under a national communications regulator.
- Claims touching market share, pricing, or competitive position require Legal/Regulatory review.
- ESG claims must align with group-verified data.
- GDPR applies to audience targeting, campaign data, and influencer data handling.
- EU AI Act, DSA, and DMA awareness is required where relevant.

AI-use limits:

- Exclude leadership-transition specifics.
- Exclude real commercial or retainer terms.
- Exclude competitor-by-name intelligence.
- Exclude unannounced strategic plans.
- Use only publicly grounded facts plus this sanitized brief.
- Treat prior unadopted agency positioning ideas as tone reference only, never approved positioning.
- Replace client and individual names with generic stand-ins or role titles.
- Replace financial specifics, budgets, and retainer terms with ranges or TBC.

## Expected Outputs

- Evidence base and readiness check: what is known, what is missing, and what must be decided before strategy can proceed.
- Positioning options: two to three reasoned territories with a recommended direction and rationale, not a single pre-baked answer.
- Corporate brand platform/message architecture: core idea, narrative, and message house framed as a first build for client decision.
- Pillar architecture: derived from evidence and argued, including how many pillars and why.
- Stakeholder and executive thought-leadership map.
- Twelve-month roadmap/campaign platform linked to business moments.
- Measurement framework aligned to AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the AMEC Integrated Evaluation Framework.

## What Good Looks Like

- Input discipline: surfaces gaps before writing and flags that positioning is undecided.
- Strategic structure: pillars and positioning are reasoned from evidence, not borrowed from competitors.
- Review trail: every recommendation traces to input and separates fact from judgment.
- Honest about unsettled decisions: presents options for client decision rather than asserting a finished answer.
- Practical first artifact: message architecture small enough for a client decision meeting, but substantive enough to test the central strategic bet.

## Safety Note

This brief uses sanitized facts plus publicly grounded context. No confidential client documents, real names, real financials, or specifics of the leadership transition are included. The strategic problem is preserved while identifying and sensitive details are removed or generalized. The account team should review anything pulled into a live demo before it runs.
